newsitem.title: CHINA: China earthquake leaves 10 dead, several injured.
newsitem.headline: China earthquake leaves 10 dead, several injured.

text.p: Two major earthquakes rocked China's westernmost Xinjiang region within a minute on Tuesday, killing at least 10 people and injuring more than a dozen, officials said.

An earthquake measuring 6.4 on the open-ended Richter scale struck the Jiashi and Artux districts at 9.47 a.m. (0147 GMT), followed by a tremor measuring 6.3, an official of the State Seismological Bureau said.
"We are measuring this as a single earthquake of 6.4," he said.

However, an official with the local seismological bureau in Jiashi said the stronger earthquake had measured at least 6.6 on the Richter scale, strong enough to inflict widespread damage in the region populated mainly by sheep herders and cotton farmers.
"It was really terrifying, people could not even keep standing up it was so powerful," said one local resident.

At least 10 people had been killed and more than a dozen injured, officials said, quoting initial reports for the Jiashi district, about 50 km (30 miles) from the mainly Moslem bazaar town of Kashgar.
The number of casualties could rise as rescue teams and officials searched through rubble of collapsed houses in the farming district around the town of Jiashi, the official said.

"We will know more later in the day as we get reports from outlying districts," the seismological bureau official said by telephone, adding that authorities were checking the extent of damage in an area with a fairly large number of sheep farmers.
Dozens of aftershocks had rocked the region and many people were afraid to return to their homes, despite freezing temperatures, another official said.

Many residents of Jiashi had spread layers of cotton felt on the ground and had snuggled into it to keep warm, he said, adding that he had only returned to his office briefly to report to his superiors.
"It was a very strong earthquake," he said. "People are all very frightened, especially with the aftershocks which seem as if they will never stop. Some are big, some are small."

The earthquakes struck as most residents were on their way to work in a region where offices open officially at 10.00 a.m., because Beijing runs all of China as a single time zone despite differences in hours of daylight.
State television said an unknown number of houses in Jiashi had collapsed and cracks had appeared in many others.
"It felt much stronger than last time," the seismological official said, referring to an earthquake of 6.9 magnitude that rocked Jiashi in March last year, killing 26 people and injuring 128.
Unlike the March earthquake when officials had sent out warnings of an impending tremor, local residents had been taken by surprise, he said.
A tremor measuring 5.0 on the Richter scale shook a remote corner of China's Tibet region on Monday.
The quake was centred in the Naqu region, about 600 km (360 miles) northwest of the regional capital, Lhasa. There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage.
